title: Trombone as humming bass part and trombone taking the lead
summary: Ridgley describes the trombone as a humming bass part with solo licks, and says the trombone could take the lead early on.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: We never did have a night at the trombone. Someone would be playing like that in dancing music. We'd learn as to bump and bump, bump, like a ba, a solo ba, ba, and so on. Until we used to rip and slide and get all that. But we used to get along. We used to like it.
Well, when you play Dixieland music, the trombone part, you say you're thinking of the bass part.

It's the humming, that's what Raleigh said, it's just the humming bass part. Humming bass part. Yeah, the trombone. See, you didn't cut it like the bass violin, but you could use more of that solo. Then you could make your add to it, too. You see, we used to add a whole lot to it.
Well, what did you think about when you added to it? Did you try to harmonize with the trumpet or did you try to play when the trumpet wasn't playing to fill in the holes?

You could do it either way. You could play along with him. You see, if you'd play along with him, then he would play like a second part on the trumpet or something like that, you see? Right. You'd be holding the lead like that, you see?
You had trombone lead early, way back. The trombone would take the lead.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Would the trombone usually have the lead instead of the trumpet? And the things that we would make, you know, get together. Or you could steal it from the orchestra, you see. You could steal a part like that from the orchestra and make your trombone part. And if you had a corner with good ears, like Lewis Armstrong, you could play a third corner. See? One of the ears, you couldn't lose that boy on the wing.
